extracted.intended_audience: computer science students, programmers writing literate programs and user manuals, and academic referees/authors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing literate programs and user manuals, plus best practices for refereeing academic papers (how to evaluate, report, and help authors improve). Covers code/module structure, exposition, typography, usability, and referee responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module length
rubrics_metrics.description: Don thinks that a dozen lines of code is about the right length for a module.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break long modules into several manageable pieces; WEB's philosophy is to decompose a complex thing into tractable parts so code should reflect small modules.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-level exposition (avoid mere step-through)
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple stepping through of the process does not qualify; we are trying to convey an intuition of what is going on, so a high-level account is much more helpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer explaining intent and intuition rather than line-by-line narration of the algorithm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readable descriptive text (avoid 'engineerese')
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid slipping into 'engineerese'—e.g., all conjunctions and no punctuation—which makes poor documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use normal punctuation and readable prose; don't imitate stream-of-consciousness or overly terse technical shorthand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct WEB formatting (begins/ends)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the formatting of begins and ends in WEB is correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Errors in WEB formatting (misplaced begins/ends) are unacceptable; follow WEB conventions precisely so the document structures correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drop obsolete conventions when changing style
rubrics_metrics.description: When you change style (e.g., to WEB), don't carry excess baggage such as adding comments like 'end {while}'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the conventions appropriate to the new style and avoid unnecessary carry-over of old notational habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification/anthropomorphization of programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Using 'I' for the computer (e.g., 'What file should I process?') can aid user conceptualization, though some (e.g., Dijkstra) dislike it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personification can make the system easier to understand, but be aware of differing opinions and be consistent in style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't start sentences with symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: As in mathematics, avoid starting a sentence with a symbol (e.g., 'data assumes that ...' should be rewritten).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite symbol-leading sentences into natural-language constructions for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-colloquial/stream-of-consciousness style
rubrics_metrics.description: While an enthusiastic, conversational style ('Oooops! How can we fix this?') may motivate reading, descriptions should still be descriptive and precise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep engaging tone but ensure clarity, accurate terminology, and avoid sloppy or imprecise descriptions (e.g., confusing 'complement' and 'component').

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment variable declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: In WEB you can declare variables at any point; Don thinks it is always a good idea to add some comment when you do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide at least a cursory explanation when declaring variables to help readers understand their purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographic care for operators (asterisks/multiplication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typeset asterisks often appear higher than typewritten ones, making multiplication expressions look odd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'x' for multiplication or use a typewriter-style font with centered '*' if necessary to avoid typographic confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group specialized routines together
rubrics_metrics.description: If a program uses a somewhat specialized data structure (e.g., the heap) unknown to readers, keep all the heap routines together in the text so they can be read as a group while fresh in the reader's mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use WEB's freedom of ordering to place related routines close together rather than scattering them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module title capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't capitalize the first letter of every word in module titles; better to follow newspaper-headline convention by leaving small words lowercase or capitalize only the first word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use natural-looking titles rather than awkward title-casing that capitalizes conjunctions/articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Font conventions for numeric representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use typewriter type for hexadecimal numbers (e.g., '3F') and leave decimal numbers in normal type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This visual distinction aids subliminal type-checking and reduces confusion between number formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: The words used in the documentation should match the words used in the formal program; using two different terms for the same thing confuses the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt consistent naming throughout prose and code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place begins/ends inside called modules
rubrics_metrics.description: Habit of putting begins and ends inside the called modules (not in the caller) is recommended; mixing the two conventions can produce appalling bugs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow one convention consistently—prefer the begins/ends inside the called module as illustrated in examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribute local variables near use
rubrics_metrics.description: Large procedures should have their local variables 'distributed' as the exposition proceeds; variables may be declared near their use in WEB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep variable declarations close to where they are used to improve readability and comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use macros to extend language where needed
rubrics_metrics.description: You can define macros (e.g., string_type(#) = packed array [1..#] of char) in WEB to simulate language features missing in Pascal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use macros judiciously to improve expressiveness and hide language limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth in Naming (nouns for data, verbs for procedures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the function determine the part of speech: verbs are for procedures, not data; prefer nouns for variables (e.g., 'place' rather than 'scan').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose names that reflect role and encourage correct mental model for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent program personification
rubrics_metrics.description: Be consistent in the use of 'it', 'we', or 'I' when personifying the program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mixing personifications across the document; consistency aids reader understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write user manuals for the truly naive user
rubrics_metrics.description: User manuals should assume no understanding of computers or of writing; the Naive User should be able to use the system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain concepts plainly, avoid implicit assumptions, and structure material so nontechnical readers succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid jargon; use accessible terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms familiar to CS people (e.g., 'Menu', 'Scrolling', 'reverse video') may mean nothing to naive users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either avoid jargon or define it in accessible terms (use 'flashing bar' instead of 'cursor' where helpful).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include 'how to get out' / recovery instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuals almost never explain how to get out of a mess if the user does something wrong; this is important to the naive user.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear, jargon-free exit and recovery instructions (explain 'EXIT' plainly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid alarming formatting like all-caps
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences like 'And now you should ENTER the data' do nothing to help the user relax—the capitals look like DANGER SIGNS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use normal-case instructions and friendly phrasing to reduce user intimidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use intuitive and mnemonic key mappings
rubrics_metrics.description: Design key mappings to be mnemonic (e.g., OPTION-N to leave bold/return to normal rather than reusing the same key to toggle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer natural mappings (OPTION-N for Normal, OPTION-B for Bold) and avoid confusing repeated toggles that are hard to discover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise sentences, friendly tone, and online demos
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep sentences short, friendly, and skimmable; inviting the user to type '?' for an online demonstration can spare long arcane descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use short paragraphs, offer interactive demonstrations where possible, and use diagrams/animations to replace verbose descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sensible defaults (inherit previous style)
rubrics_metrics.description: When prompting for parameters repeatedly, defaults should preferably be the style used for the preceding line rather than fixed defaults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimize repetitive input by carrying forward reasonable defaults to reduce user effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual structure: overview, step-by-step, diagrams, keyboard guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Best manuals have a good overview, step-by-step descriptions, crisp sentences, easy-to-skim layout, helpful redundancy, diagrams, and keyboard diagrams that explain which keys to use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate control-key usage clearly (holding vs typing), use icons for scrolling directions, and include diagrams for complex actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain ambiguous messages clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid obscure notes like '!THIS IS VISIBLE HERE BUT NOT HERE'; instead explain in plain language (e.g., 'Extra long messages can be seen if you make them move').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace cryptic labels with simple, explanatory sentences that describe behavior or action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendly encouragements sparingly and appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments like 'Good luck!' and 'Enjoy!' are good; odd reassurances ('this system has been carefully redesigned not to bite') are not reassuring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use encouraging language where appropriate but avoid unintentionally alarming or trivializing phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refereeing primary criterion: originality
rubrics_metrics.description: The first criterion should be originality; is the material presented a genuine advance on previous work?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the paper contributes new ideas/results or is merely rehashing known results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee responsibility to authors and readers (be a teacher)
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees should see their primary responsibility as being to authors and readers, not just to editors; try to supply constructive criticism and help authors improve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-critical, anonymous nastiness; provide guidance, references, and improvements that raise the paper's quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supply references and improve technical content
rubrics_metrics.description: A referee can contribute by giving references to related work the author missed or by improving results (even anonymously contributing theorems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point to missing literature, suggest corrections, and where appropriate offer technical improvements or checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose journals for quality of referees
rubrics_metrics.description: When selecting a journal, prefer one with the best referees rather than the least critical editor; authors want to know if they truly made a contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look at a journal's practice and prior handling of related subjects to judge likely quality of review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refereeing decision categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers generally fall into: (1) Publish essentially as is; (2) Publish after author's minor revision; (3) Publish only if the author makes major revisions (re-refereed); (4) Reject (nothing salvageable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to improve papers; rarely place a paper in category 1 unless it truly needs only trivial typographic edits. If recommending rejection, suggest alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core referee evaluation checklist (a–d)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) The paper should contribute to the state of the art or be clearly designated as expository. (b) All technical material must be accurate (check equations carefully). (c) The article must be understandable, readable, and written in good English. (d) The bibliography should be adequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these four points as the backbone of the referee report: correctness, significance/exposition, clarity/style, and adequate referencing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of referee reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not postpone refereeing; the refereeing cycle is 'critical path time' in publication. Return the report promptly—if you cannot referee, tell the editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit the report quickly (text suggests within a week or at most a few weeks); if unable to referee, inform editor immediately to avoid delaying publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript handling and reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Return the manuscript to the editor (do not mark it up); you may write a separate confidential letter to the editor; submit in duplicate; you may choose whether to reveal your name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow editorial procedures: don't annotate author copies, provide clear separate report(s), and adhere to submission formats requested by the journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggest alternative journals on rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: When recommending 'Reject', referees are asked to suggest a less prestigious journal that might publish the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide constructive direction to help the author find an appropriate venue rather than simply dismissing the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cooperative, not legalistic
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees should act to improve papers cooperatively (a correspondence among experts) rather than adopting a legalistic stance focused on careers over science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor constructive, community-minded review that raises standards of exposition and correctness.
